body.statement:
Let \(j\in\{1,2\}\), and let \(Q_j\) be any Borel probability law on \(\mathbb R\) satisfying \(\int |u|^{q_e}\,dQ_j(u)\le M_e\), where \(q_e>1\).  Then
\[
 |\phi_{Q_j}(t)|\ge 1-|t|M_e^{1/q_e}\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).
\]
Consequently, for \(\nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1}\) and \(c_*=1/2\),
\[
 \inf_{|t|\le\nu_*}|\phi_{Q_j}(t)|\ge c_*.
\]
body.proof_tex:
The probability normalization gives \(\phi_{Q_j}(0)=1\).  Lyapunov's inequality, whose present one-dimensional form follows from Jensen's inequality applied to the concave map \(z\mapsto z^{1/q_e}\), gives
\[
 \int |u|\,dQ_j(u)
 \le\left\{\int |u|^{q_e}\,dQ_j(u)\right\}^{1/q_e}
 \le M_e^{1/q_e}.                                                \tag{1}
\]
For real \(v\), the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \(|e^{iv}-1|\le|v|\).  Hence the reverse triangle inequality and (1) yield, for every real \(t\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\phi_{Q_j}(t)|
 &\ge 1-|\phi_{Q_j}(t)-1|\\
 &\ge 1-\int|e^{itu}-1|\,dQ_j(u)\\
 &\ge 1-|t|\int|u|\,dQ_j(u)
 \ge 1-|t|M_e^{1/q_e}.                                          \tag{2}
 \end{aligned}
\]
If \(|t|\le\nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1}\), the last member of (2) is at least \(1/2=c_*\), proving the claimed uniform protected neighborhood.
